title: High-Latency Metadata Indexing
business: A digital archive service managing millions of document metadata records that must be retrieved by unique identifiers.
problem: Standard binary search trees result in excessive disk I/O because the tree height is too large, forcing multiple slow storage reads to traverse from root to leaf.
solution: A B-Tree stores many ordered keys per node, which significantly increases the branching factor and reduces the total tree height, ensuring that metadata lookups require fewer disk accesses.
steps: Define a node capacity that aligns with the underlying storage block size to optimize I/O.
Insert keys into nodes while maintaining sorted order within each node.
Split nodes when they reach maximum capacity to maintain balance.
Promote the median key to the parent node to facilitate efficient searching.
outcome: Improved retrieval latency for metadata lookups due to a shallower tree structure and minimized disk seek operations.
limitation: The primary tradeoff is increased memory usage per node and complexity in handling node splits and merges; monitor this by tracking the average node occupancy ratio.

questions.question: In High-Latency Metadata Indexing, why is a B-Tree preferred over a standard binary search tree?
options: It reduces tree height and storage reads by storing many keys per node.
It eliminates the need for disk I/O entirely.
It automatically sorts data by insertion time.
It uses less memory than a binary search tree.
questions.explanation: The business problem specifically identifies excessive disk I/O due to tree height, which the B-Tree solves by increasing the branching factor.
questions.evidence: A B-Tree stores many ordered keys per node, which significantly increases the branching factor and reduces the total tree height, ensuring that metadata lookups require fewer disk accesses.

questions.question: In High-Latency Metadata Indexing, what is the primary tradeoff associated with the B-Tree implementation?
options: Increased node split frequency leads to permanent data loss.
Increased memory usage per node and complex maintenance logic.
The tree height increases linearly with the number of keys.
It requires more disk I/O than a binary search tree.
questions.explanation: Storing multiple keys per node requires more memory per node and logic to manage splits and merges, which is a known tradeoff.
questions.evidence: The primary tradeoff is increased memory usage per node and complexity in handling node splits and merges; monitor this by tracking the average node occupancy ratio.
